senses: A practitioner or adherent of irrationalism.
One who is irrational in their beliefs or ideas.
Adorned with gimp (decorative trim); edged or embroidered.
Jagged, as a jagged or uneven edge or outline; notched, edged with serrations or grooves; nicked, dented.
Crippled, injured; damaged as to awkwardly impede function.
examples: The leaves... are slightly “gimped,” and this gives them an apparently wavy outline.
Then he wheeled him around and began pushing him lickety-split down the hall, the chair's rickety wheels squealing like a gimped grocery cart.

senses: Universal in scope.
examples: In tracing the relationships between Western Modernism and the arts of Africa, Oceania and the Americas, the curators took a universalist approach.

senses: The condition of being a continent.
The degree to which the climate of a place is affected by a large land mass.
The idea that people learn about, or perceive the world by constructing mental models.
examples: But is it one constructionism in many guises, or a variety of quite different constructionisms, or merely old issues dressed up in new jargon,
The futility of dismissing social constructionism in favor of some "real," authentic nature outside the social and linguistic.

senses: An aircraft that performs airlifts.
examples: The C-5 entered service in 1970 and is the biggest airlifter in the U.S. inventory.

senses: To prepare (something) for winter weather.
To remove the saturated fats from (a vegetable oil) by cooling and filtering it, so that it does not become cloudy in the winter.
examples: Temperatures are expected to plummet over the weekend, and aside from grabbing a coat, experts say there’s some things you should do to winterize your home.

senses: The status or term of office of a pontiff or pontifex.
ety: From Latin pontificatus, from pontifex (“high priest”), from pons (“bridge”) + facere (“make”).

senses: A group of warriors or nobles accompanying a king or other leader.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from Latin comitatus, from comes (“companion”). Doublet of county, from Anglo-Norman/Old French.

senses: The regions in which a sheriff has authority.
The office, or period of office, of a sheriff.
examples: Crossing the river got him beyond his old nemesis' sheriffdom and into the territory of a more liberal authority.
For the purposes of the administration of justice, Scotland is to be divided into areas, each to be known as a “sheriffdom”.
His sheriffdom began with his election and ended with his death.

senses: Situated or happening outside of the blood vessels or lymph vessels.
A bearing of a rhomboidal figure, originally representing a spindle in shape, longer than a heraldic lozenge.
ety: From Middle English fusill, from Old French fusel, fuisel, from a late Latin diminutive of Latin fūsus (“spindle”).

senses: Having two conditions
A post on an internet site, especially associated with being terminally online or causing mischief.
ety: Probably first attested in c. early-2010s, but in common usage only as of the late 2010s. The spelling variant seems unexplained and may just be fanciful, or deliberately childish (compare memes like fren and groyper).

senses: A pat on the head, typically as a sign of affection.
A native or inhabitant of Sodom.
ety: From Middle English sodomyte, sodomite, from Old French Sodomite and Latin sodomīta, from Ancient Greek σοδομίτης (sodomítēs). Equivalent to Sodom + -ite.

senses: A Hebrew measure of itinerant distance: one parsa is about four kilometers, approximately the distance a man can walk in 72 minutes; a parasang.
Housefly excrement, visible as a minuscule black dot.
Anything tiny or insignificant.
examples: The wall of the kitchen above the fruitbowl was dotted with flyspeck.
From the foothills below, Jean, Jan, and James were mere flyspecks, easily lost among the straggly pines that formed the treeline.
We passed through some flyspeck town, barely more than a gas station and a stoplight, but I never saw the name.

senses: A traditional one-piece dress worn by Chinese women.
ety: From the Hanyu Pinyin romanization of the Mandarin 旗袍 (qípáo).

senses: A person, device, or agent that presses or squeezes, as
A member of a press-gang, who forces (presses) others into service.
A person or device that removes wrinkles, usually from clothing.
examples: Visiting a traditional vineyard, we watched the grape pressers treading the grapes underfoot.
That's the name of the people who make the polystyrene compound used by pressers of records that don't warp.
He saw the man who did the cleaning and pressing for the hotel, a man whom he had always seen before in the gloom of the pressing shop sweating over a steam presser.

senses: A groom who specializes in palfreys or good quality riding horses.
examples: His war needs were heavy. In 1330 his stable staff included 29 carters, 37 sumptermen and 92 palfreymen.

From the early fourteenth century onwards, the hospital employed a cook and his assistant, along with an assortment of hired hands, including a laundress, a palfreyman, a boatwright, a smith and a swineherd.

senses: The area of practical theology which studies the mandate, message and work of the Christian missionary.
That which thickens.
Any substance added to something in order to thicken it; a thickening agent; a binder.
examples: This is a new twist, a plot thickener.

senses: To trim or abridge by cutting off parts.
ety: From French vaisseau rasé, from raser (“to rase, to cut down ships”). See raze and rase (verbs).

senses: Strict adherence to a given form of conduct, practice etc.
An approach to interpretation and/or evaluation focused on the (usually linguistic) structure of a literary work rather than on the contexts of its origin or reception.
The tendency to elevate formal above expressive value in music, as in serialism.
The ontological view of mathematics as a mere collection of string manipulation rules.
A documentary about rock music or its musicians.
examples: The first 30 minutes or so of "Metallica" have the flavor of a standard behind-the-scenes rockumentary.
It occasionally suffers from the pontification so deservedly satirized in rockumentaries like This Is Spinal Tap.

senses: To have more people than (one's competitor); to outnumber in men.
To outdo in manliness.
examples: The United States dominated, and then in extra time outworked the outmanned Mexicans, with Jozy Altidore and Donovan setting up Bradley’s second goal.

senses: Of or resembling glass; glassy.
Having a shiny nonporous surface.
ety: From Middle French vitreux, from Latin vitreus (“glassy, transparent”), from vitrum (“glass”). The terms vitreous (positive) and resinous (negative) electricity were coined in 1733 by Charles François de Cisternay du Fay, who studied the different behaviour of glass and resin when rubbed with silk and fur, respectively.

senses: Any fuel that is obtained from a renewable biological resource, especially from biomass.
Synonym of chronometric, of or related to horologia and horology.
ety: From horologic + -al. Equivalent to horo- + logical or horology + -ical.

senses: A situation in which a player is forced to make a disadvantageous move; a position where any legal move will worsen a player's situation.
A situation in which someone is forced to make a disadvantageous move.
ety: From German Zugzwang, from Zug (“move”) + Zwang (“compulsion”).

senses: Easily offended; apt to be annoyed.
Something which retards or slows.
A refrigerator used to slow down proofing of yeast when making dough.
examples: The substance acted as a retarder to the chemical reaction because it radically changed the pH.
Why is retarder used in dope when the dope is being sprayed in humid conditions? The retarder slows the drying of the dope and keeps it from blushing.

senses: Someone who lives well.
Producing a noise or effect like thunder; thunderous.
Very great; extraordinary.
ety: From Middle English thonderynge, þoundryng, equivalent to thunder + -ing.

senses: A mid-sized horse used to pull a bus.
The performer in music who takes the accompanying part.
to sieve; sift; riddle
ety: From Middle English riddren, from Old English hridrian, from Proto-Germanic *hrīdrōną (“to sieve; sift”), from the noun. See above.

senses: A teacher who uses plausible but fallacious reasoning.
One who is captious, fallacious, or deceptive in argument.
Synonym of sophister (“university student who has completed at least one year”).
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin sophista and sophistes, borrowed from Ancient Greek σοφιστής (sophistḗs, “wise one”), from σοφίζομαι (sophízomai, “to become wise”).

senses: A person who asks questions, or who conducts an official enquiry.
ety: From Middle English questioner; equivalent to question + -er.
